ApiError.description:
Typed, because SPEC: client-shared-surface requires every client to
distinguish auth failure from an unknown calendar from an out-of-range
query, and it cannot if the server returns prose.

A type rather than a pre-built `Response`, so that handlers can `?` their
way through parsing and the failure path reads as short as the success one.

error.description: A stable machine-readable tag. Clients switch on this, never on prose.

as_of.description:
RFC 3339. Answer from the dataset Diurn was serving at that instant
(Enterprise).

kinds.description: One character per date, in the order of `dates`.

verification.description:
Likewise. Present on every row: it is the cheap half of provenance and
the half that decides whether to trust the cell (SPEC: provenance-is-stored-not-shipped).

BulkResponse.description:
Column-oriented: the dates once, then one short code per day per calendar.

For 150 calendars over a year that is 54,750 cells. Spelling them
`"open"` would be half a megabyte of the same word; the legend is
returned with the payload so the compaction costs no documentation.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

venues.description:
One series per requested MIC, keyed by the MIC.

**Deliberately one per venue, even when several share a calendar.** Four
US equity MICs answer identically and still get four series. The
alternative — one row per internal calendar, with a map from MIC to
row — is what this used to be, and it published the grouping: which
venues we consider equivalent is the modelling, and it is ours. It also
let a client key on an id that is unstable by design, since a calendar
gets split the moment a venue is found to be answered wrongly.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

count.description:
Trading days in the range, inclusive. **A lower bound when `unknown`
is above zero**: those days may trade.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

unknown.description: Days in the range the engine cannot answer.

DataWindow.description: The dates the plan may ask about, from today (UTC). Null is unbounded.

DatasetServed.description: The dataset that answered an `as_of` request (SPEC-pricing §5.1).

id.description:
First twelve hex of the dataset's content id: what `/health` calls
`dataset`, and the same for every build of the same data.

reconstructed.description:
True for a model rebuilt after the fact rather than served at the
time. Nothing is rebuilt yet, so this is false.

served_until.description: When the next dataset replaced it; null while it is still served.

oneOf.description:
Which products got which day, in the venue's own words. Sent exactly
when `kind` is `open_for_some`, and the only account of the split there
is — see [`DayKindDto::OpenForSome`].

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

DayResponse.description: One day, and with `as_of`, which dataset answered.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

as_of.description:
RFC 3339. Answer from the dataset Diurn was serving at that instant
(Enterprise).
With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

days.description:
The days of the kinds asked for, by date and then MIC. No provenance:
ask for the day itself.

artifact.description:
First twelve hex of the served artifact's SHA-256, or `"built-in"` for
the copy baked into the image.

**This is here so "which artifact is this process serving" can be
answered without a shell on the instance.** `diurn-ops datasets` prints
the same twelve characters beside each row, so the two can be compared
directly — and a server stuck on an old dataset shows up as a checksum
that is not the active one, rather than as a `built_at` somebody has to
recognise. A server once sat a day behind through four publishes and the
only symptom was a timestamp nobody could place.

dataset.description:
First twelve hex of the served dataset's content id: what its data
says, without when it was built. The same for every build of the same
data, which `artifact` is not, and the name the point-in-time archive
uses (SPEC: point-in-time-archive).

mapped_venues.description:
How many MICs this process can answer for by explicit mapping.

It used to report how many *calendars* were loaded, which is the one
unit no external caller is given a name for (SPEC: everything-is-keyed-by-mic).
A venue count is both free of that and the
more useful number: it says how much of the answerable surface this
artifact covers, where the calendar count says how many groupings we
happen to keep behind it.

registry_published.description: Publication date of the ISO vintage this process is serving.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

at.description:
`null` when the engine cannot say — past an anchor's range, beyond the
scan horizon, or on a calendar that publishes no hours at all, as
`US-FUTURES-ICE` does. Not the same as "never".

This is the intraday axis, so a `null` here says nothing about whether
the venue trades: ask `/v1/trading-days`, which answers from the day's
kind rather than from whether hours were authored.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

JointSkipped.description:
A date passed over: the venues that did not trade it, other than for a
weekend.

as_of.description:
RFC 3339. Answer from the dataset Diurn was serving at that instant
(Enterprise).
With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

skipped.description:
Dates passed over on which some venue was closed other than for a
weekend.

unknown_skipped.description:
With `on_unknown=skip`: dates passed over uncounted because the answer
for them is unknown.

venues.description: Each venue's kind of day on `date`.

MicWindow.description:
One MIC cap's count (SPEC-pricing §6.4). `max` is null on a plan with
every MIC.

mics.description:
The MICs in the window: listed for the 24-hour one, so a caller can
see what holds their slots.

resets_at.description: When the oldest MIC in the window leaves it, freeing a slot.

allowed.description: For `out_of_window`: the dates the plan may ask about; null is unbounded

mics_in_use.description: The MICs holding the window's slots

resets_at.description: When a slot frees, the budget renews, or the rate allows another request

ProductSplitDto.description:
Which products traded on a day that did not treat them alike.

The venue's own name for each group, never our internal id: the calendar
files a split by declared id so it can be checked and so two readings of one
page compare equal, and `canola` means nothing outside that file.

note.description:
What the lists cannot carry — a venue saying some hours will be
announced later, which leaves a group open and its hours unknown.

Provenance.description: The evidence behind a day. Only ever sent when asked for.

ResolutionDto.description:
How a MIC reaches its answer (SPEC: calendar-membership). The MIC pages
state the same.

kind.description:
`own`: the venue is answered directly. `operating_mic`: through its
operating MIC. `country`: through the one calendar for its country.
The last two are inferences, not checked claims.

via.description: The MIC or country that answers.

products.description:
Which products these hours are for, in the venue's own words. **Absent
means the whole venue**, which is almost every calendar.

The same field `SessionDto` carries and for the same reason (SPEC
4.3.30) — it reached `/sessions` first and stopped there, which left the
gap this closes: *"is it open now"* is precisely where a scope matters
most. Cboe C1 runs an overnight book scoped to four symbols, so a
caller asking at 03:00 was told `running` with `name` — a label this
project chose — and had no way to learn that C1 being open said nothing
about an ordinary equity option (SPEC: one-mic-two-venues).

trade_date.description:
The day this session belongs to, which may not be the day it started on.

**Do not derive this from `close`, even though you can.** A session's
close is always stamped on its trade date and only its open is ever
shifted back, so the trade date really is `close`'s date *in the venue's
zone* — an invariant a regression test pins across the whole dataset.
The trap is that every venue shipped today closes at a local time whose
UTC date is the same, so a client that slices the first ten characters,
or reads the UTC date, is correct against all of them and will stay
correct until the first session closing after midnight local lands. ICE
publishes one — Singapore 16:45–01:30, which closes at 17:30Z the
previous day — and it is queued for `US-FUTURES-ICE`.

Served rather than left implicit for that reason, and because it is the
session's identity: it is what a caller joins on against trade and
settlement data, and what every dated route on this API is keyed by.
It appears here and not on `day.sessions[]`, where it would only ever
repeat `day.date`.

open.description:
RFC 3339, in the venue's own zone. A session close is a zoned instant,
never a naive local time.

products.description:
Which products keep these hours, in the venue's own words. **Absent
means the whole venue**, which is almost every calendar and every
session on it.

Present, it is the only thing that tells two sessions apart. ICE
Futures U.S. serves thirteen on an ordinary day — two of them closing
at the same minute — and without this a caller has `name`, which is a
label this project chose and not the venue's. "When does cocoa trade"
had no answer on the wire while the dataset knew it (SPEC: hours-need-a-citable-sentence).

The venue's own name, never the declared id the calendar files it
under: `canola` is a key that means nothing outside that file, and
`ProductSplitDto` states the same rule for the day axis.

SkippedDay.description: A day stepped over: not a weekend, and not trading.

StateDto.description:
Whether the venue is trading **at an instant** — the intraday axis.

A real enum rather than three string literals chosen in an `if`, so that the
OpenAPI document enumerates the values, the generated clients get a union
type instead of `string`, and a test can assert the set has not drifted. Its
sibling [`DayKindDto`] was always typed this way; this was not, and the
asymmetry was invisible until somebody tried to write that test.

**No value here is shared with [`DayKindDto`] except `Unknown`**, and that
one is deliberate: past the resolvable horizon both axes go quiet, and
`day.kind` is what tells the two apart (SPEC: two-resolutions). Every other
overlap would be a word meaning different things in one response.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

day.description: The civil day the instant falls on, in the venue's zone.

mic.description: Present when the request was keyed by MIC rather than by calendar.

oneOf.description:
The session running at `at`, if one is.

**A different question from `day.sessions`, not a copy of it.** That
field is the *schedule* — what this civil date's trade date holds. This
one is the *instant* — what is live right now, and which trade date it
belongs to. They coincide whenever `at` falls inside a session owned by
the civil day, which for a cash market is most of the time, and that
makes the two look redundant. Each is the only carrier of the answer in
some case:

| `at` | `day.sessions` | `running` |
|---|---|---|
| Frankfurt, mid-session | the session | the same session |
| CME, Sunday 23:10Z | absent — the day is a weekend | Globex, `trade_date` Monday |
| Tokyo, at lunch | morning and afternoon | absent |
| Frankfurt, before the open | the session | absent |

The futures row is why this field exists at all: at 17:00 on a Sunday in
Chicago, CME is open, and the civil day is a weekend with no sessions of
its own because the running session belongs to Monday's trade date. Both
are true, and a response carrying only the first reads like a
contradiction. The Tokyo row is why `day.sessions` cannot be dropped in
exchange: between the two sittings nothing is running, and the schedule
is the only thing that says an afternoon exists.

Named `running` rather than `session` because sitting beside
`day.sessions` the shorter name read as the same noun.

state.description:
`running`, `closed`, or `unknown`. **Not a boolean**: a day the engine
cannot compute is not a closed one, and collapsing the two is the
failure that loses trust.

This is the **intraday** answer. `unknown` covers both ways of being
unable to give one — a date past the resolvable horizon, and a day that
certainly trades on a calendar with no authored hours — and the day
question is answered separately by `day.kind`, which stays confident in
the second case. A caller who only needs *does trading happen* should
read that, or `/v1/trading-days`, and never this.

as_of.description:
RFC 3339. Answer from the dataset Diurn was serving at that instant
(Enterprise).
With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

skipped.description:
Non-trading days passed over that are not weekends: why the answer is
where it is.

TradingDaysResponse.description:
A date and whether the venue trades on it, and nothing else.

The shape a time series wants. `/v1/sessions` answers "what kind of day is
this, and how much do you trust it"; plenty of callers only want to index a
DataFrame by trading day and are indifferent to the rest.

as_of.description: With `as_of`: the instant asked about. Absent otherwise.

oneOf.description: With `as_of`: the dataset that was being served then, which answered.

dates.description:
The dates once, in order, shared by every venue below. Columnar rather
than pairs because the endpoint takes many venues, and pairs would
repeat the dates for each — and because `zip(dates, trading)` is one
line in every language that would ask for this.

venues.description:
One series per requested MIC. See [`BulkResponse::venues`] for why they
are not deduplicated.

trading.description:
`true` when any session runs — an early close and a shortened holiday
session both count, because the venue does trade.

**`null` when the engine cannot say.** Past an anchor's range, or on an
unconfirmed advisory date, there is no answer, and returning `false`
would tell a caller the market is shut when what we mean is that we do
not know (SPEC: timeline-view). It is rare — a range inside the
confirmed horizon has none — and `unknown` counts them so a caller can
assert zero and forget about it.

UsageView.description:
An account's usage against its plan (SPEC-pricing §6.4): what
`GET /v1/usage` answers, and what the account page shows.

oneOf.description: Null on a plan without a venue-day budget.

VenueDay.description: One venue's day, in a row-oriented list.

resets_at.description: The start of the next billing month.

products.description:
The product schedules the venue's answers distinguish, in the venue's
own names. Empty for almost every venue.

oneOf.description: How the venue reaches its answer. Absent when no calendar answers it.

timezone.description:
The IANA zone the venue's sessions are quoted in. Absent when no
calendar answers the venue.

VenueStatus.description:
One venue's entry: `StatusResponse` without the `at` the response states
once.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `cursor` for the next page; null on the last.

VerificationDto.description: How much to trust a served day. Always present.

key.description: An API key, `diurn_key_…`. Free at https://diurn.io/signin/.

info.description:
Market calendars and trading hours, with provenance.

Every day carries a `verification` status — `verified`, `corroborated` or `inferred` — which is never optional. The evidence behind it, `source` and `retrieved`, is fetched with a single day or with `expand=provenance` on the range endpoints, on plans that include it, and is deliberately absent from the bulk endpoints.

**Keys and plans.** Every endpoint but the registry record, `/health` and this document needs a key: `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, free at https://diurn.io/signin/. A plan limits the unique MICs requested in a rolling 24 hours and 30 days, the dates it may ask about (a forward horizon and a history depth); Enterprise's MICs are uncapped. Every metered response reports usage in its `Diurn-MICs-Day`, `Diurn-MICs-Month` and `RateLimit-*` headers, and `GET /v1/usage` reports it in full. The rules: https://diurn.io/docs/limits/ Plans and prices: https://diurn.io/pricing/

get.description: The same query as `/v1/sessions`, reduced to the one question a time series asks: does this venue trade that day. `true` includes early closes, a shortened holiday session, and an `open_for_some` day where only part of the venue traded — in each case the venue does trade. A caller who needs the partial days separated must ask for the days themselves and read `products`. One series per requested MIC, as above.

get.summary: Every day in a range for a venue

get.description:
`state` is `running`, `closed` or `unknown`, and answers the **intraday** question. It is not a boolean: a day the engine cannot compute is not a closed one. `unknown` also covers a day that certainly trades at a venue whose hours are not published — ICE Futures U.S. publishes no citable session times, so *whether* it trades on a Tuesday is not in doubt and *when* is. `running` rather than `open` because `open` is a *day* kind, and a venue is routinely `closed` at an instant on a day whose kind is `open`. The day question is answered by `day.kind` here, or by `/v1/trading-days`, and neither goes `unknown` for that reason.

`running` and `day.sessions` are different questions rather than a copy. `day.sessions` is the **schedule** — what this civil date's trade date holds. `running` is the **instant** — what is live at `at`, and which trade date owns it. They coincide whenever `at` falls inside a session belonging to the civil day, which for a cash market is most of the time, and that is why they can look redundant. Each is the only answer somewhere: at 17:00 on a Sunday in Chicago the day is a weekend with no sessions of its own and `running` carries Globex on Monday's trade date, while at lunch in Tokyo nothing is running and only `day.sessions` shows that an afternoon sitting exists.
